content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes fairness measurement techniques for generative models. In existing work, the bias of (unconditional) generative models are evaluated using pre-trained attribute classifiers. This work points that these generative models are inaccurate, so whatever bias is measured may not be meaningful for evaluation. Next, a solution (CLEAM) is proposed where the idea is to use a statistical model for classifier outputs. Experiments on manually labeled datasets show that CLEAM has much less error compared to baselines.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths
- Identifies a critical problem in existing fair generative model works and proposes an intuitive fix. Inaccurate pre-trained attribute classifiers are really problematic because they may give a distorted picture on the performances of existing fair generative model works.
- The proposed method CLEAM is able to significantly reduce the fairness measurement error by using a statistical model for classifier outputs.
- Creates new datasets by manually labeling the GAN-generated samples.

Weaknesses
- The presentation of the paper can be improved. There seems to be too much coverage on how existing methods do not accurately measure bias (first 5 pages!) and too little coverage on the solution (next 2 pages). I would have been already convinced by the first contribution if the authors just showed that [Choi et al., 2020]'s pre-trained model had low accuracy according to the manually-labeled datasets. [Choi et al., 2020] actually mentions this very problem as future work in Section 6: Discussion. Just saying that this work addresses that problem would have made things pretty clear early on.
- It is not clear why the proposed statistical model is the best model. While I agree that having probability distributions instead of single values contains more information, why should we assume a multivariate Gaussian distribution? Do other statistical models result in worse performance? 
- In Section 4, computing the point estimate for p* seems to be going back to computing single values. How is this approach fundamentally superior to the existing fairness measurements?
- In the experiments, only using one dataset (CelebA) is a bit underwhelming. While I understand [Choi et al., 2020] also only uses CelebA, this work is about identifying the universal problem of how fairness measurement techniques are incorrect. If possible, it would be good to verify the claims on datasets like MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, CIFAR, and ImageNet as well.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
- The problem is important as it is about a bug in previous works.
- The ideas are clear, but the presentation can be improved.
- The technical depth itself is a bit shallow without enough justifications.
- The experiments should be done on more datasets.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall, the paper identifies an important blind spot in existing fair generative model works where the evaluation itself is problematic. The solution of using statistical models makes sense as having a probability distribution contains more information than single values. However, the paper itself can be improved especially in terms of presentation, technical depth, justifying its statistical model, and experiments.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper studies the problem of fairness measurement in generative models (more specifically image generation domain). It first, talks about the effects that inaccuracies in the classifiers used in these measurement approaches has on the reported measures then proposes a measurement framework CLassifier Error- Aware Measurement (CLEAM) that is more aware of the inaccuracies in the classifiers.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
**Strength:**
1. The datasets created in this work can benefit the community.
2. Code and material is provided which makes the reproducibility aspect strong for this work.

**Weaknesses:**
1. The writing and organization of the paper needs drastic improvements. There are multiple references to the Appendix and generally, it is not easy to follow and stay engaged with the paper which can make reading the paper boring and not interesting.
2. I did not find the first contribution of the paper that interesting and something very novel to discuss about although the majority of the paper is focused on the first contribution which in my opinion is nothing surprising.
3. The findings and application is really limited to this use-case or proposed way of measuring bias in generative models. What if we propose other metrics not relied on the classifier at all?
4. Maybe related to my above comment, if you studied other areas in fair generation the paper would have been more interesting considering more diverse use-cases and measures.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: Overall, I found the paper relatively poor in terms of clarity, quality and novelty. The paper can improve drastically by improving the writing and organization to keep the reader more engaged and interested. The quality as well can improve if authors considered more diverse use-cases and discussions. The first finding which was occupying most of the paper, was not something novel and interesting. With that being said the paper did a good job with regards to the reproducibility aspect.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall, I think the paper has some merits including the dataset collected in this work and the approach; however, the first contribution and the limited discussions makes the paper less interesting for the reader.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper studies the fairness in generative models where a classifier is leveraged to estimate the group probabilities. This paper identifies the issues of inaccurate estimation caused by inaccurate classification results. Then, a simple statistical method is developed to recover the group probabilities of a generative model from the inaccurate prediction.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:

+. This paper studies a very interesting problem where inaccurate prediction poses challenges in measuring the unfairness of generative models.
+. A simple statistical approximation method is proposed to obtain a stable and accurate estimation of the GT probabilities.
+. Two datasets are created from generated images.

-. There is a gap between GT probabilities and fairness. The results are reported for the estimation of p_0. However, the unfairness is p_0-p_1 (for binary prediction). If the estimation error is symmetric, the error of unfairness might be small. It would be more convincing if the methods are evaluated with regard to unfairness.
-. The proposed CLEAM method assumes the estimation of GT follows a Gaussian distribution for s batches but it also assumes the classifier has consistent performance for all batches, that is the correct/wrong classification probability is fixed. These two assumptions are controversial. The classifier is trained and fixed. But each batch has slightly different data points. So the estimation is considered as a random variable. Thus, the correct/wrong predictions are also various.
-. The CLEAM method requires a knowledge of the classification accuracy alpha. If my understanding is correct, alpha is derived from the validation set of other datasets instead of the generated images. It is unclear whether the alpha values are the same for these datasets. In another word, it is unclear whether an inaccurate alpha value matters for CLEAM.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: This paper is easy to read but the notations are too many and a little bit confusing.
content.summary_of_the_review:
The problem is very interesting. Given an imperfect classifier, the fairness assessment for a generative model is inaccurate. It is very necessary to develop solutions for this problem. This paper makes a step to estimate the GT probabilities from a classifier.

However, there are some technical concerns about this paper. The proposed method assumes the correct/wrong prediction rates are consistent and fixed for s batches, which is unusual. In addition, the classifier performance is different among datasets. The alpha values from existing datasets cannot be used as a true and precious estimation for this newly generated dataset.

There is a small gap between group probabilities and unfairness metrics.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The authors highlight the measurement error in existing fair generative model metrics and propose a new framework using point and interval estimates of biases of generated data.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths: 
1. The authors compare several different architectures that may exhibit classifier errors and demonstrate the effectiveness of CLEAM on all of them. 

Weaknesses: 
1. Attribute classifiers seem to be not as great. For example 0.801 for true negatives on a binary classification like hair or gender? How does the accuracy/quality of the classifier affect the error in estimation? For example, ResNet-34 and MobileNetv2 look similar in terms of $\alpha$ but the errors are larger in one and not the other. 
2. It would be useful to see what $\rho_{Base}$ is directly for Table 1: it is not clear to me whether the difference in error magnitude between the first 3 classifiers is statistically significant. 
3. It would be great to see a discussion on classifier errors. Are the generated samples too OOD for the classifiers? Are there too many hard samples? It is difficult to tell from human annotations whether the classifiers just do not generalize to generated examples or whether the examples were just harder. Appendix 5 describes the protocol of inclusion: a majority vote of 3 labelers was selected but it is hard to understand this without context. For example, for the real training dataset, what level of agreement is achieved among annotators? 
4. The authors compare to existing work from 2019 and thus use “fairness” notions from then. While this is acceptable for the purpose of this paper, I think this work could be strengthened by using better terminology and adding discussion introduced by more recent and nuanced fairness work in representation and diversity. For example, what would error mean if diversity was measured across continuous attributes like age? 

Nit:
1. Table 1: Resnet-35 StyleGAN gender has an extra “]” bracket
2. Equation 8: why are you using the biased variance estimator? Why not use the empirical variance estimator? 

Questions: 
1. It looks like (from Table 1) $\hat{p}$ always underestimates $p^*$. Is it really measurement error or is there just a biased estimation happening somewhere?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: Overall paper was written clearly and the diagrams were helpful. No obvious quality or reproducibility issues since they are introducing a measurement method. I am not aware of existing work that uses their new method of measuring diversity.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall this paper does a good job of investigating errors in existing diversity measurement methods for generative models. While the method suggested by this work of incorporating point and interval methods is not the most novel, I think it will be quite useful for the community. I am not sure how much a 4-5% estimation error really matters in practice. But I can imagine when intersectional groups are introduced down the line, 4-5% could be the entire subpopulation.

content.title: On Fairness Measurement for Generative Models
content.abstract: Deep generative models have made significant progress in improving the diversity and quality of generated data. Recently, there has been increased interest in fair generative models. Fairness in generative models is important, as some bias in the sensitive attributes of the generated samples could have severe effects in applications under high-stakes settings (e.g., criminal justice, healthcare). In this work, we conduct, for the first time, an in-depth study on fairness measurement, a critical component to gauge the research progress of fair generative models. Our work makes two contributions. As our first contribution, we reveal that there exist considerable errors in the existing fairness measurement framework. We attribute this to the lack of consideration for errors in the sensitive attribute classifiers. Contrary to prior assumptions, even highly accurate attribute classifiers can result in large errors in fairness measurement, e.g., a ResNet-18 for Gender with $\sim$97% accuracy could still lead to 4.98% estimation error when measuring the fairness of a StyleGAN2 trained on the CelebA-HQ. As our second (major) contribution, we address this error in the existing fairness measurement framework by proposing a CLassifier Error-Aware Measurement (CLEAM). CLEAM applies a statistical model to take into account the error in the attribute classifiers, leading to significant improvement in the accuracy of fairness measurement. Our experimental results on evaluating fairness of state-of-the-art GANs (StyleGAN2 and StyleSwin) show CLEAM is able to significantly  reduce fairness measurement errors, e.g., by 7.78% for StyleGAN2 (8.68%$\rightarrow$0.90%), and by 7.16% for StyleSwin (8.23%$\rightarrow$1.07%)} when targeting the  Gender attribute. Furthermore, our proposed CLEAM has minimal additional overhead when compared to the existing baseline. Code and instructions to reproduce the results are included in Supplementary.
